sentences.text: The 33 sermons on Nibbana were delivered by the Venerable Bhikkhu Kathukurunde Jnanananda in Sinhala at Mitrigala Nisarana Vinaya Forest Hermitage.
They were translated into English by the same Venerable monk, presently residing at Potkulkala Forest Hermitage in Khandagedra Devalagam.
Namutase Bhagavata Rahata Sammha Sambuddhase
Namutase Bhagavata Rahata Sammha Sambuddhase
Namutase Bhagavata Rahata Sammha Sambuddhase
This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the stealing of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.
With the permission of the most venerable great preceptor and the assembly of the venerable meditating monks, this is the tenth fifth sermon in the series of sermons on Nibbana.

The other day we made an attempt to understand, in the light of the Kalakarama Sutra, the enlightened attitude of the Tathagata, who has realized the cessation of the six bases of sense contact towards the viewpoints of the worldlings, who find themselves confined within those six bases.

In that discourse, the Buddha declared with the words Tamahan Janani, all that I do know, the fact that he has understood all what the world with its gods, Maras and Brahmas, and the Prajini consisting of recluses and Brahmins, gods and men, have seen, heard, sensed, organized, thought after and pondered over by the mind.
By his next assertion, Tamahan Abhanyasin, the Buddha proclaimed that he not only knows all that, but knows it thoroughly in some special way.
If the words Tantathagata Savidhitam, he declares that by virtue of this special knowledge, he has understood all what the world claims to know.

Despite this special knowledge and understanding, the Tathagata takes no stance, and has no inclination, no partiality towards those sensory data, as is evident from the expression, Tantathagato na upatthasi.

Wordlings, in general, are in the habit of asserting dogmatically, I know, I see, it is very so, Janani, Karsami, Tathayvayetam, when they have a special knowledge or understanding of something or other.

But according to this discourse, it seems that the Buddha takes no stance, and has no inclination, no partiality towards those sensory data, precisely because he has a special knowledge and understanding with regard to him.
This fact is highlighted by the concluding summary verses, particularly by the lines,
In order to explain this strange difference of attitude, we quoted the other day, two significant terms from the Moola Pariyasutta of the Majjhmanikara, namely, Sanyanati and Abhijanati.
They represent two levels of knowledge in the context of that particular discourse.
Sanyanati stands for perceptual knowledge, whereas Abhijanati conveys the idea of some special understanding of a higher order.
The level of knowledge implied by the term Sanyanati is that which characterizes the ordinary worldling's worldview.
He is deluded by the Mirad-like perception in his view of the world, and goes on imagining, Manjana, the real world enslaved to the patterns of the geometrical structure.
But that the Tathagata has penetrated into the true nature of those seen, heard, sensed and the life, it is extraordinary level of higher knowledge, Abhijanati, yielding full comprehension.
Therefore, he does not take his stand upon any of them, he has no stance to justify the usage of the term Upatthasi, since he does not entertain imaginings.
What is called Manjana is the imagining in egoistic terms, imparting reality to illusory things.
It is this principle of refraining from vain imaginings that is indicated by the term Naupatthasi, does not take his stand upon.
Tathagatas have no clinging or entanglement, Ajhosita, precisely because they entertain no imaginings.
In regard to things seen, heard, etc., the Tathagatas have no clinging, binding or entanglement by way of craving, conceit and lives respectively.

We happen to mention the other day that those peculiar declarations with which the Kalakarama Sutta opens bear some resemblance to the tetralemma discussed in our treatment of the undetermined points.
The set of four alternative propositions concerning the Tathagatas' after-death state may be cited as a paradigm for the tetralemma.
1. Hoti Tathagato Parammarana. The Tathagata exists after death.
2. Na Hoti Tathagato Parammarana. The Tathagata does not exist after death.
3. Hoti Can Na Chahoti Tathagato Parammarana. The Tathagata both exists and does not exist after death.
4. Nema Hoti Na Na Hoti Tathagato Parammarana. The Tathagata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
The declarations found in this discourse bear some affinity to the above-mentioned tetralemma.
However, we find here the Buddha making the first declaration in several stages.
5. Firstly, he makes the statement that whatever is seen, heard, sensed and cognized, thought after and pondered over by all beings in the world, that he knows.
6. In the second statement he affirms that he has a higher knowledge of all death.
7. Then comes a sentence which reaffirms that the Tathagata has understood, but ends with the statement that the Tathagata does not take his stand upon it.
8. Generally, when confronted with the Tetralemma, the Buddha summarily dismisses all the four alternative propositions.
9. But here the peculiarity is in not dismissing the first proposition at once.
10. He declares that he knows, that he has higher knowledge and that he has understood all that.
11. Apparently he is affirming the first proposition, granting the validity of sensory data.
11. But then comes the concluding statement to the effect that he does not take his stand upon them, no pathasi, which amounts to a negation.
11. The secret behind this peculiar presentation will emerge when we bring up the proportionaries and parables.
12. Till then, what can be gleaned from the context is that the Tathagata has no stance, not because he is ignorant,
12. but due to the very fact that he knows full well and has understood the nature of the sum total of sensory data.
12. The worldlings are prone to think that it is when convincing knowledge is lacking that one has no such stance.
13. But the Buddha declares here that he takes no stance in regard to what is seen, heard, sensed, etc.,
13. precisely because he has a special understanding, a penetrative knowledge of the essencelessness of the data obtained through the sixth sense basis.
14. So it seems, in this context too, we have the negation of the first ordinary way, as is usual in the case of a tetralema,
15. only that the negation is expressed here in a very peculiar way.
15. Let us now take up the second declaration.
15. If I were to say,
15. Whatsoever in the world with its gods, maras and brahmas,
16. among the prajini consisting of recluses and brahmins, gods and men,
16. whatsoever is seen, heard, sensed and cognized, thought after and pondered over by the mind,
16. all that I do not know, it would be a falsehood in me.
16. There is a difference of opinion as to the correct reading of this second declaration.
16. Deep suttas often present difficulties in determining the exact reading,
16. and this especially the case with the khargaram suttas.
17. In this instance, the commentary has followed the reading,
17. Tamaham jana viti vadayam tamamasa musa.
18. If I were to say that I know, it would be a falsehood in me.
18. But as we have pointed out earlier, this reading is not meaningful.
18. That is probably why the chhattasangeeti pitak edition has followed the variant reading,
18. tamaham najana amiti vadayam, if I were to say that I do not know.
19. This departure from the commentary of tradition seems justifiable,
since the Buddha has already declared that he knows all that.
19. It stands to reason, therefore, that in the second declaration he makes it clear that to say,
19. A, I do not know, would be a contradiction, a falsehood.
19. A falsehood
But why this clarification?
Generally, the worldlings expect one to unequivocally assert and take one's stand upon one's viewpoint in categorical terms,
as expressed by the dictum Idhami-va-satyang-mohga-manyam.
This alone is true, all else is false.
Failure to do so is recognized as a lack of knowledge or precision.
The second declaration is meant to forestall such an objection.
Since the first declaration ends with the clause tam tathagato na uparthasi,
but the tathagata has not taken his stand upon it.
So it amounts to a statement like,
it is not because I do not know that I take no stance.
In the same strain, we can explain the declarations that follow.
It seems then that the second declaration, tamang na jana miti vadeiyam tam namassa musa,
if I were to say all that I do not know, it would be a falsehood in me,
amounts to the second alternative of the tathagata.
The next declaration follows the same trend.
To quote the relevant portion, tamang jana miti nana cha jana miti vadeiyam tam passi tathagata.
If I were to say I both know it and do not know it, that too would be a falsehood in me.
If I were to say that I know, I do not know, or even a combination of both those statements,
as I both know and do not know, it would be a falsehood on my path.
Why? Because the world is accustomed to put down such a reconciliation to a lack of certitude.
To say I both know it and know it not, looks like a confession of partial knowledge,
since it can mean knowledge and ignorance going fifty-fifty.
So the Buddha says in this instance too, that it would likewise be a falsehood.
Now we come to the fourth statement. The Buddha declares,
If I were to say I neither know it nor am ignorant, it would be a falsehood in me.
tamang nevajana miti vadeiyam tamang asakari.
We can understand that position too.
Generally the worldlings think that a refusal to make a categorical statement
is either due to partial knowledge or to an attitude of wriggling out.
In fact, this attitude of wriggling out had already assumed the status of a philosophy in itself
in Sanjay Beratti Buddha, a contemporary of the Buddha.
When he was interrogated, he would respond with such a series of negations like,
I do not say it is, I do not say it is thus, I do not say it is otherwise, nor do I say it is neither, etc.
The attempt here is to evade the issue by a sort of ill-ribbling.
That school of philosophy which resorted to such an evasive legerdiment came to be known as Amaravikhaipavad.
The Buddha refuses to subscribe to such tactical sophistry by rejecting the fourth alternative.
I neither know it nor am ignorant of it.
Here then we have the same tetra jama, presented in a different guise.
It smacks of a riddle that the Buddha was confronted with, the riddle of coming to terms with worldly parlance.
As we have already mentioned, the commentary analyzes the main theme of the discourse into five planes.
It also records that the earth shook at five points of the discourse, that is, at the end of the proclamation for each plane.
According to the commentary, the first plane is the plane of omniscience,
Sambanyatabhu.
The phrases representative of that plane are said to be,
Tamahang janami, that I know.
Tamahang ambhanyasi, that I have I fully understood.
And Tantathagata sabiditam, that is known to the Tathagata.
Then comes the plane of the influx-free one, Khinasabhu,
represented by the section ending with the phrase Naupattasi,
does not take his stand upon it.
It is so called because that phrase brings out the characteristic of not taking a stance by way of cravings,
conceits and bivs, in the case of an influx-free one.
The three phrases, Tantamama as Musa, it would be a falsehood on my part,
Tampasatagisameva, likewise that too would be a falsehood in me,
and Tantamama as Sakhali, it would be a fault in me,
are interpreted by the commentary as representing the third plane of truth, Satchabhu.
We have now dealt with that too.
What comes next as the fourth plane is the deepest of all.
The commentary calls it the plane of the void, Sunyatabhu.
It is with good reason that it is so good.
The paragraph that follows is said to represent that plane.
It runs.
This is what it is.
Here, too, we are confronted with the question of variant readings.
To begin with, here we have given the phrase Ditta Dattabbang Ditta,
whereas the commentary takes it as Datta Dattabbang Ditta.
According to the commentary, Datta is a hypothetical variant of the absolutive form Disva,
for it paraphrases Datta Dattabbang Ti Disva Dattabbang.
That is, Datta Dattabbang stands for Disva Dattabbang.
So the whole sentence in question is said to convey the sense,
having seen, he does not imagine a seen worth seen.
But the variant reading Ditta is granted,
though the commentator prefers the reading Datta,
as it is suggestive of an absolutive Drishtva.
Taking the cue from this commentarial preference,
the Burmese Chatta Sangeet edition goes a step further
in substituting Sutva, Mutva and Vinyatva rather arbitrarily
to give an absolutive twist to the three phrases that follow,
as Sutva Svotabbang Sutam, Mutva Motabbang Mutam,
and Vinyatva Vinyatabbang Vinyatam.
Probably the editors thought that in this context the terms Ditta, Sutta, Mutva and Vinyatva could not be interpreted as they are.
But we may point out that in keeping with the line of interpretation we have followed so far,
these three terms may be said to stand for an extremely deep dimension of this discourse dealing with the one.
The other day we simply gave a sketch of a possible rendering.
The statement Ditta Rattabbang Vittangamanyati has to be interpreted as an assertion
that the Tattagata does not imagine a sight worth while seeing as apart from the seeing,
that there is nothing substantial in the seeing.
So also the other statements, Sutta Svotabbang Sutamamanyati does not imagine a worthwhile hearing apart from the heard.
Mutamotabbang Mutamamanyati does not imagine a worthwhile sensing apart from the sensed.
Vinyatavinyatabbang Vinyatamanyati does not imagine a worthwhile cognition apart from the cognized.
In case our interpretation still appears problematic, we may hark back to the Bahiya Sutta we have already explained at length.
The philosophy behind the Buddha's exhortation to the ascetic Bahiya could be summed up in the words,
Ditta, Ditta, Matanbhavisati Sutta, Matanbhavisati Mutimu,
Matanbhavisati Vinyatva, Vinyatva, Matanbhavisati.
In the seeing there will be just the seeing, in the heard there will be just the heard,
in the sense there will be just the sensed, in the cognized there will be just the cognized.
What is meant is that one has to stop at just the seeing,
without discursively imagining that there is something seeing, something substantial behind the seeing.
Similarly, in regard to the heard, one has to take it as just a heard, not something heard.
In the case of the face, Ditta, Dattabbang Ditta, Lamanyati, the word Ditta being in the ablative case,
we may render it as, does not imagine a sight worthwhile seeing as apart from the seeing.
By way of further clarification of this point, we may revert to the simile of the dog on the plank,
which we gave in our explanation of Namarupa.
The simile, of course, is not canonical but of fabled origin.
When a dog, while crossing a stream, stops halfway on the plank
and starts wagging its tail and peeping curiously down,
the reason is the sight of its own image in the water.
It imagines a dog there, a water dog.
The dog thinks that there is something worthwhile seeing apart from the seeing.
It is unaware of the fact that it is seeing what it sees because it is looking.
It thinks that it is looking because there is something out there to be seeing.
The moment it realizes that it is seeing because it is looking,
it will stop looking at its own image in the water.
We have here a very subtle point in the law of dependent and right.
One that is integral to the analysis of the human form.
So then, due to the very ignorance of the fact that it is seeing because it is looking,
the dog imagines another dog there in the water.
What is called manjana is an imagining of that sort.
No such imagining is there in the tathāgata.
ditta da tampang ditta na manjata.
He does not imagine a sight worth seeing as a part from the scene.
In short, for him, the scene is the be-all and the end-all of it.
The scene is dependently recent.
It comes about due to a collocation of conditions,
apart from which it has no existence per se.
Every instance of looking down at the water is a fresh experience,
and every time an image of the dog in the water and of another looking at is created.
The dog is seeing its own image.
Everything is dependently recent.
Pascha pascha, says the brahma jala sutta.
Dependent on context.
Here there is something really deep.
It is because of the personality view, sakkaya rittu,
that the world is carried away by this illusion.
One goes on looking saying that one is doing so as there is something to be seen.
But the scene is there because of the looking.
This then is the moral behind the statement ditta da tappang ditta na manjata.
does not imagine a scene worthwhile scene as apart from the scene itself.
This is the dictum implicit in the bahaya sutta too,
which could be illustrated by the simile of the dog on the planet.
The tappang ditta does not imagine a sight as existing apart from the bare act of seeing.
If further illustrations are needed, let us take the case of hearing music from a distance.
One imagines a thing called music and with the idea of listening to the same music,
goes to the place where the music is going on.
One is not aware of the fact that at each step in that direction one is hearing a different music.
Why?
Because one is ignorant of the dog dependent arising.
Just as in the former case, the dog seeing is dependent on the dog looking.
Here too, the auditory consciousness of a music is the outcome of a dependence between ear and sound.
So, deluded as he is, he goes to the music hall to listen better to the same music.
He will realize the extent of his delusion if he happens to put his ear to the musical instrument.
When he does so, he will hear not a music, but a set of crude vibrations.
But this is what is going on in the world.
The world is steeped in the delusion of imagining that it is the same music one is hearing.
Though at each step in that direction, the music changes.
This is due to the fact that it is dependent on the ears.
Actually, there is no person hearing, but only a state of affairs dependent on the ear and sound.
A conditioned arising dependent on contact.
In the present textual context, the terms ditta, sutta, mutta and vinyata, seen, heard, sensed and cognized have to be understood in this light.
So, this is how the phrase ditta, ditta and vinyata, has to be interpreted.
But the commentary does not seem to have appreciated the relevance of this paragraph to the Buddha's teachings on voigness.
While commenting on ditta namanyati, it expatiates,
aang maja nena ditta meva pasamiti tanna vana ditti namanyati.
According to it, what is meant is that the Tathagata does not imagine, by way of cravings, conceits and gives,
that he is saying just what the common people have seen.
This is an oversimplification, a rather shallow interpretation.
The next phrase, aditta namanyati, is similarly explained.
Aditta namanyati ti aang maja nena ditta meva etang pasamiti evaampi tanna di manyanahi namanyati.
He does not imagine and unseen means that the Tathagata does not imagine, by way of imagining, through craving, etc.,
that he is saying something unseen by the common people.
The commentary, it seems, has gone at a tangent, bypassing the deeper sense.
We have already explained the deeper significance of the phrase ditta namanyati.
Does not imagine the scene.
Now what does aditta namanyati mean?
In terms of our simile of the dog on the planet,
ditta namanyati means that the Tathagata does not imagine a dog in the water.
Aditta namanyati could therefore mean that the Tathagata does not imagine that the dog has not seen.
Why he does not treat it as an unseen should be clear from that declaration we had already decided,
ending with tamaham na janamiti vadejaṁ tammamāsa musa.
If I were to say that I do not know, it would be a falsehood in me.
The fact of seeing is not denied, though what is seen is not taken as a dog but only as an image of one.
That is dependently arisen.
Since the understanding of it as a dependently arisen phenomenon is there,
the Tathagata does not imagine an unseen either aditta namanyati.
The phrase ditta namanyati is also explicable in the light of the foregoing discussion.
Now, the dog on the plank keeps on looking down at the water again and again
because it thinks that there is something worthwhile seeing in the water.
Such a delusion is not there in the Tathagata.
He knows that at its turn it is a phenomenon of a seeing dependent on contact, possible way.
Every time it happens, it is a fresh sight, a new preparation, sankhāra.
So there is nothing to look for in it.
Only a looking is there, nothing worth looking at.
Only a seeing is there, nothing to be seen.
Apart from the bare act of hearing, there is nothing to be heard.
It is the wrong view of a self that gives a notion of substantiality.
The above face ditta is suggestive of insubstantiality, senselessness and whiteness.
Music is just a word.
By taking seriously the concept behind that word, one imagines a thing called music.
The pandemonium created by a number of musical instruments is subsumed under the word music.
Then one goes all the way to listen to it.
The same state of affairs prevails in the case of the seeing.
It is because the Sathagata has understood this fact that he does not imagine a thing worth seeing or hearing.
The same applies to the other sensory data.
Then comes the phrase that thārana manyati does not imagine a fear.
Here we have the direct expression of whiteness.
The whiteness of a self or anything belonging to a self.
Now that dog on the plank has not understood the fact that there is a mutual relationship between the looking dog and the seeing dog.
It is because of the looking dog that the seeing dog is seen.
There is a conditioned relationship between the two.
In other words, dependent on eye and forms arises eye consciousness.
The mere presence of the eye is not enough for eye consciousness to arise.
But dependent on eye and forms arises eye consciousness.
Though stated simply, it has a depth that is not easy to fathom.
To say that it is dependent on eye and form is to admit that it is dependently a reason.
The law of dependent arising is already implicated.
There is therefore no seer apart from the phenomenon of seeing according to the Dathagata.
He does not imagine a seer, Datharana manyati.
For the worldly, the bare act of seeing carries with it the perception of one who sees.
He has a notion of a self and something belonging to a self.
The same teaching is found in the Bahya Sutta.
After instructing Bahya to stop at just the seeing, the heard, the sensed and the cognized,
the Buddha was going to outline the end result of the training.
If you cannot do this similar, you are not bakesh.

You must be shark.

This is the end of stopping.
That is to say, when Bahaya, you have gone through that training of stopping at just the seed, the herd, the sensitive and the colonized,
then you would not be imagining in terms of them.
The algebraic life expressions, Natena and Natatha, have to be understood as forms of egoistic energy, Mannyana.
When you do not imagine in terms of them, you would not be in them.
There would be no involvement in regard to them.
In the case of that music, for instance, you would not be in the orchestra.
The egoistic imagining implicating involvement with the music presupposes a here, Svotaram, dwelling in the orchestra.
When Bahaya, you do not dwell in it, Yathothang Bahaya, Natatha, then Bahaya, you are neither here nor there nor in between the two.
This example is the end of suffering.
In other words, you would have realized wildness.

The expressions that Tarang Namanyati does not imagine here, Svotaram Namanyati does not imagine here, Mottaram Namanyati does not imagine sense, and Minyatara Namanyati does not imagine know, have to be understood in this light.
The Sathagata does not even imagine a thinker apart from thought.
This is the plane of the void, Sunyatabhumi, the perfect realization of the calllessness or senselessness of the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the connerged.
The very absence of Mannyana or egoistic imagining is to be understood by Sunyatabhumi or the plane of the void.
The world link takes seriously the subject-object relationship in the grammatical structure, as it seems the simplest explanation of phenomena.
Because there is something to be seen, there is someone who sees.
Because there is someone who sees, there is something to be seen.
There is a duality between these two.
To understand the law of dependent and rising is to be free from this duality.
It is the ability to see a concatenation of conditions, a conglomeration of causal factors, an assemblage instead of a bifurcation.
The way of the world links, however, is to follow the subject-object relationship, a naive acceptance of the grammatical structure, which is the easiest mode of communication of ideas.
They are misled by it to take seriously such notions as one who sees and a thing sees, one who hears and a thing hears, but the Tathagata is free from that delusion.
Now we come to the fifth section of the discourse, known as Thadibhumi, the plane of the Satch.
It runs,
It runs,
Ittikhova bhikkaveta Tathagato, ditta suttam utta vinyat, abbe sudhammesu, thadhi eva thadhi, tamma cha pana thadhi, maa anyo thadhi, uttari tharova, panita tharova, natthi ki vadami.

Thus, months, the Tathagata, being such in regard to all phenomena, seen, heard, since then, colonized, is such. Moreover, than he who is such, there is none other higher or more excellent, I declare.

The most difficult word here is thadhi. We have already explained it to some extent. It can be rendered by such or thus. The commentary explains it by the phrase, thadhi tanama eka sadhi sattha. Suchness means to be always alike.
By way of illustration, the commentary states, Tathagato cha yadhi so la bhaadhi so thadhi so va ala bhaadhi so. As he is in regard to gain, etc., so is the Tathagata in regard to loss, etc.
The allusion here is to the eight worldly vicious institutes. Gain, loss, fame, ill-fame, praise, blame, and pleasure, pain.
But this explanation is rather misleading, as it ignores a certain deep dimension of the meaning of the term Thadhi.
When it is said, as he is in regard to gain, so is he in regard to loss. One can ask, how is he in regard to gain? This is imprecise as a meaning.
However, the commentator happens to quote from the Mahanidesa another explanation, which is more to the point.
It is briefly stated as, it ta nitte tadhi, such in regard to the desirable and the undesirable, and explained as,
la bhae pi tadhi, ala bhae pi tadhi, yase pi tadhi, yase pi tadhi, nindaya pi tadhi, pasansaya pi tadhi, sukhe pi tadhi, dukhe pi tadhi.
He is such in gain, as well as in loss. He is such in fame, as well as in ill-fame, etc.
That is the correct explanation.
Instead of saying, as he is in gain, so is he in loss.
We have here continuous suchness in regard to all vicious institutes.
He is such in gain, as well as in loss. He is such in fame, as well as in ill-fame.
He is such in praise, as well as in blame. He is such in pleasure, as well as in pain.
The reason for this suchness we have explained on any other occasion.
In one sense, the term tadhi stands for the understanding of the norm called tatata.
The other implication is the abstinence from the tendency towards identification or acquisition, meant by tammyata.
This exemplary trait is called atammyata. This is an extremely important term occurring in the discourses, which however has fallen into neglect at present.
In the case of music, for instance, tammyata would imply an attachment to it that amounts to an identification with it.
Tammyo means made of debt, as in suvanname, made of gold, and rajatame, made of silver.
To be free from this tammyata is to be tadhi, such, that is to say, not to be of that stuff, a tammyata.
The attitude of not leaning on or grasping is meant by it.
The quality of being tadhi or such is often rendered by firmness, steadfastness, and immobility.
Generally, one associates firmness, immobility, or stability with holding on or leaning on.
But here we have just the contrary.
Not to hold on to anything is to be such.
This sadness has a flexibility of a higher order when adaptability.
The adaptability characteristic of the sage who lives on Pindapatha, O'am's wood, is highlighted in the following verse.
Suppose I got it, well and good. Suppose I didn't get it, that's fine too.
In both circumstances, he is such and comes back like one who walks up to a tree.
This kind of adaptability and resilience is also implied by the term tadhi.
Though the term is sometimes rendered by the word steadfast, it does not stand for any rigidity.
Instead, it carries implications of a non-rigid resilience.
This is a wonderful quality in the tathagatas and aham.
We will compare it to a revolving swing in a children's playground.
One who is seated in a revolving swing has nothing to get upset about falling headlong when the swing goes up.
The seats are hung in such a way that they also turn with the revolving motion of the swing.
Had they been rigidly fixed, one seat at there would fall off the seat when it goes up.
It is that kind of resilience that is characteristic of the quality of tadita, or suchness.
This is how we have to understand the famous line Sintamahamangara Sutta,
whose mind remains unshaken when touched by worldly resistives.
This quality of being unshaken, this immobility, is the result of not grasping.
It comes when there is no tenacious clinging.
It is to one who rests on or leans on something that there is dislodgement or instability.
Now I am leaning on the wall.
For example, if someone does damage to the wall, I would get shaken.
That is what is suggested by the axiom Nisitasa Charita, Anisitasa Charita Nati.
To one who is attached, there is dislodgement.
To the one detached, there is no dislodgement.
The wordling, on the other hand, thinks that to lean on or to rely on something is the mark of stability.
